images.label: MacConkey agar
images.commonsTitle: File:Lactose fementing (LF), and non-lactose fermenting (NLF) colonies on MacConkey agar.jpg
images.description: MacConkey agar is a selective and differential medium used to isolate and differentiate Gram-negative bacteria, particularly those belonging to the family Enterobacteriaceae. It's primarily used to distinguish between lactose-fermenting (LF) and non-lactose-fermenting (NLF) colonies. Here's what you can typically observe on MacConkey agar: Lactose-Fermenting (LF) Colonies- Appearance: LF colonies

images.label: Pseudomonas pigment
images.description: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a nonfastidious, Gram-negative (Fig. J), oxidase postive (Fig. H), nonfermenting rod. P. aeruginosa produces pyoverdin , a water-soluble yellow-green pigment (Fig. A, C, D1, D2). Many P. aeruginosa strains also produce the blue pigment pyocyanin (Fig. B, F). When pyoverdin combines with pyocyanin, the bright green color characteristic of P. aeruginosa is created (Fig. C).

images.label: Cocci in chains
images.commonsTitle: File:Gram positive cocci in chains of Streptococcus agalactiae.jpg
images.description: Unlike Staphylococcus species that form clusters, Gemella morbillorum usually arranges itself in chains or pairs. This is due to the way the cocci divide and remain attached to each other in a line. The length of these chains can vary.
